Dolar przez lata na przemian umacniał się i słabł wobec innych walut, a jedna taka faza trwała zwykle kilka lat. To główna waluta handlu i surowców, więc jego kurs zwykle szedł w parze z cenami surowców, wynikami rynków wschodzących i wartością zagranicznych aktywów w złotych. Aplikacja patrzy na indeks dolara DXY (dolar wobec koszyka głównych walut): umacnia się, gdy indeks jest nad średnią z 200 sesji i zyskał w pół roku ponad 3 %; słabnie przy odwrotnym układzie. Teraz: słabnie · krzywa odwrócona. Słabnący dolar obniża wartość aktywów w USD liczoną w złotych i zwykle sprzyja rynkom wschodzącym oraz surowcom wycenianym w dolarach.

The dollar is weakening. Short bonds pay more than long ones, which in the past was often a warning sign.

Over the years the dollar has alternately strengthened and weakened against other currencies, and one such phase usually lasted several years. It is the main currency of trade and commodities, so its exchange rate usually went together with commodity prices, emerging market results and the value of foreign assets in zloty. The app looks at the dollar index DXY (the dollar against a basket of major currencies): strengthening when the index is above its 200-session average and gained over 3% in six months; weakening in the opposite case. Now: weakening · inverted curve. A weakening dollar lowers the value of USD assets in zloty and usually favors emerging markets and dollar-priced commodities. The curve is inverted: 3-month bills yield more than 10-year bonds, which usually weighs on bank margins and lending.

The stock market goes through cycles: bull markets (long periods of gains), corrections (drops of 10-20%) and bear markets (drops of at least 20% from the peak). Bull markets usually lasted several years, bear markets usually from a few months to about a year and a half. The app looks at the global stock ETF ACWI: a bull market when the price is above a rising 200-session average; a correction on a drop of 10-20% from the peak of the last year, a bear market on a drop of 20% or more. Now: correction · inverted curve. Global stocks are 10-20% below their peak of the last year: falling prices usually weigh on investor sentiment and riskier markets. The curve is inverted: 3-month bills yield more than 10-year bonds, which usually weighs on bank margins and lending.

The stock market goes through cycles: bull markets (long periods of gains), corrections (drops of 10-20%) and bear markets (drops of at least 20% from the peak). Bull markets usually lasted several years, bear markets usually from a few months to about a year and a half. The app looks at the global stock ETF ACWI: a bull market when the price is above a rising 200-session average; a correction on a drop of 10-20% from the peak of the last year, a bear market on a drop of 20% or more. Now: correction · inverted curve. Global stocks are 10-20% below their peak of the last year: falling prices usually weigh on investor sentiment and riskier markets. The curve is inverted: 3-month bills yield more than 10-year bonds, which usually weighs on bank margins and lending.

The app looks at the global stock ETF ACWI: a bull market when the price is above a rising 200-session average; a correction on a drop of 10-20% from the peak of the last year, a bear market on a drop of 20% or more. Now: bull market. Global stocks are above a rising 200-session average: a lasting uptrend usually favors growth stocks and riskier markets.

A bond yield is the yearly return on lending money to a government; the 10-year US Treasury yield is the benchmark for the cost of money worldwide. The yield curve compares long bonds with short ones: long ones usually yield more, and when short ones yielded more (an inverted curve), it often came before a US recession in the past, though not always. The app looks at the 3-month change of the 10-year US Treasury yield: a move of at least 0.40 pp up means rising yields, down falling ones; it measures the curve as the difference between 10-year bonds and 3-month bills. Now: yields falling. Lower yields lower the cost of money: they usually favor growth stock valuations and long-term bond prices.

Over the years the dollar has alternately strengthened and weakened against other currencies, and one such phase usually lasted several years. It is the main currency of trade and commodities, so its exchange rate usually went together with commodity prices, emerging market results and the value of foreign assets in zloty. The app looks at the dollar index DXY (the dollar against a basket of major currencies): strengthening when the index is above its 200-session average and gained over 3% in six months; weakening in the opposite case. Now: no trend · inverted curve. The dollar index has no clear trend: neither the six-month change nor the 200-session average points one way. The curve is inverted: 3-month bills yield more than 10-year bonds, which usually weighs on bank margins and lending.

Commodities (oil, gas, metals, crops) have their own multi-year cycles of rising and falling prices. A long wave of gains is called a supercycle: the last one came in the first decade of the 21st century, when demand from China grew fast. The app looks at a broad commodity basket, the ETF DBC: a commodity bull market when the price is above its 200-session average and over 10% higher than a year ago; a commodity bear market in the opposite case. Now: commodity bear market. A broad commodity basket is below its 200-session average and over 10% lower than a year ago: falling commodity prices usually weigh on commodity and mining companies.

US bond yields are rising, so borrowing money is getting more expensive.

A bond yield is the yearly return on lending money to a government; the 10-year US Treasury yield is the benchmark for the cost of money worldwide. The yield curve compares long bonds with short ones: long ones usually yield more, and when short ones yielded more (an inverted curve), it often came before a US recession in the past, though not always. The app looks at the 3-month change of the 10-year US Treasury yield: a move of at least 0.40 pp up means rising yields, down falling ones; it measures the curve as the difference between 10-year bonds and 3-month bills. Now: yields rising. Higher yields raise the cost of money: they usually weigh on growth stock valuations and long-term bond prices.

The app looks at the global stock ETF ACWI: a bull market when the price is above a rising 200-session average; a correction on a drop of 10-20% from the peak of the last year, a bear market on a drop of 20% or more. A bond yield is the yearly return on lending money to a government; the 10-year US Treasury yield is the benchmark for the cost of money worldwide. The yield curve compares long bonds with short ones: long ones usually yield more, and when short ones yielded more (an inverted curve), it often came before a US recession in the past, though not always. The app looks at the 3-month change of the 10-year US Treasury yield: a move of at least 0.40 pp up means rising yields, down falling ones; it measures the curve as the difference between 10-year bonds and 3-month bills. Now: yields rising. Higher yields raise the cost of money: they usually weigh on growth stock valuations and long-term bond prices.

Now: weakening. A weakening dollar lowers the value of USD assets in zloty and usually favors emerging markets and dollar-priced commodities.

A bond yield is the yearly return on lending money to a government; the 10-year US Treasury yield is the benchmark for the cost of money worldwide. The yield curve compares long bonds with short ones: long ones usually yield more, and when short ones yielded more (an inverted curve), it often came before a US recession in the past, though not always. The app looks at the 3-month change of the 10-year US Treasury yield: a move of at least 0.40 pp up means rising yields, down falling ones; it measures the curve as the difference between 10-year bonds and 3-month bills. Now: yields rising. Higher yields raise the cost of money: they usually weigh on growth stock valuations and long-term bond prices.

A bond yield is the yearly return on lending money to a government; the 10-year US Treasury yield is the benchmark for the cost of money worldwide. The yield curve compares long bonds with short ones: long ones usually yield more, and when short ones yielded more (an inverted curve), it often came before a US recession in the past, though not always. The app looks at the 3-month change of the 10-year US Treasury yield: a move of at least 0.40 pp up means rising yields, down falling ones; it measures the curve as the difference between 10-year bonds and 3-month bills. Now: yields rising · inverted curve. Higher yields raise the cost of money: they usually weigh on growth stock valuations and long-term bond prices. The curve is inverted: 3-month bills yield more than 10-year bonds, which usually weighs on bank margins and lending.

A bond yield is the yearly return on lending money to a government; the 10-year US Treasury yield is the benchmark for the cost of money worldwide. The yield curve compares long bonds with short ones: long ones usually yield more, and when short ones yielded more (an inverted curve), it often came before a US recession in the past, though not always. The app looks at the 3-month change of the 10-year US Treasury yield: a move of at least 0.40 pp up means rising yields, down falling ones; it measures the curve as the difference between 10-year bonds and 3-month bills. Now: yields falling. Lower yields lower the cost of money: they usually favor growth stock valuations and long-term bond prices.

A bond yield is the yearly return on lending money to a government; the 10-year US Treasury yield is the benchmark for the cost of money worldwide. The yield curve compares long bonds with short ones: long ones usually yield more, and when short ones yielded more (an inverted curve), it often came before a US recession in the past, though not always. The app looks at the 3-month change of the 10-year US Treasury yield: a move of at least 0.40 pp up means rising yields, down falling ones; it measures the curve as the difference between 10-year bonds and 3-month bills. Now: yields falling. Lower yields lower the cost of money: they usually favor growth stock valuations and long-term bond prices.

A bond yield is the yearly return on lending money to a government; the 10-year US Treasury yield is the benchmark for the cost of money worldwide. The yield curve compares long bonds with short ones: long ones usually yield more, and when short ones yielded more (an inverted curve), it often came before a US recession in the past, though not always. The app looks at the 3-month change of the 10-year US Treasury yield: a move of at least 0.40 pp up means rising yields, down falling ones; it measures the curve as the difference between 10-year bonds and 3-month bills. Now: yields rising. Higher yields raise the cost of money: they usually weigh on growth stock valuations and long-term bond prices.

A bond yield is the yearly return on lending money to a government; the 10-year US Treasury yield is the benchmark for the cost of money worldwide. The yield curve compares long bonds with short ones: long ones usually yield more, and when short ones yielded more (an inverted curve), it often came before a US recession in the past, though not always. The app looks at the 3-month change of the 10-year US Treasury yield: a move of at least 0.40 pp up means rising yields, down falling ones; it measures the curve as the difference between 10-year bonds and 3-month bills. Now: yields rising · inverted curve. Higher yields raise the cost of money: they usually weigh on growth stock valuations and long-term bond prices. The curve is inverted: 3-month bills yield more than 10-year bonds, which usually weighs on bank margins and lending.

The app looks at the global stock ETF ACWI: a bull market when the price is above a rising 200-session average; a correction on a drop of 10-20% from the peak of the last year, a bear market on a drop of 20% or more. Now: bull market · inverted curve. Global stocks are above a rising 200-session average: a lasting uptrend usually favors growth stocks and riskier markets. The curve is inverted: 3-month bills yield more than 10-year bonds, which usually weighs on bank margins and lending.

A bond yield is the yearly return on lending money to a government; the 10-year US Treasury yield is the benchmark for the cost of money worldwide. The yield curve compares long bonds with short ones: long ones usually yield more, and when short ones yielded more (an inverted curve), it often came before a US recession in the past, though not always. The app looks at the 3-month change of the 10-year US Treasury yield: a move of at least 0.40 pp up means rising yields, down falling ones; it measures the curve as the difference between 10-year bonds and 3-month bills. Now: yields falling. Lower yields lower the cost of money: they usually favor growth stock valuations and long-term bond prices.

Commodities (oil, gas, metals, crops) have their own multi-year cycles of rising and falling prices. A long wave of gains is called a supercycle: the last one came in the first decade of the 21st century, when demand from China grew fast. The app looks at a broad commodity basket, the ETF DBC: a commodity bull market when the price is above its 200-session average and over 10% higher than a year ago; a commodity bear market in the opposite case. Now: commodity bear market · inverted curve. A broad commodity basket is below its 200-session average and over 10% lower than a year ago: falling commodity prices usually weigh on commodity and mining companies. The curve is inverted: 3-month bills yield more than 10-year bonds, which usually weighs on bank margins and lending.

The stock market goes through cycles: bull markets (long periods of gains), corrections (drops of 10-20%) and bear markets (drops of at least 20% from the peak). Bull markets usually lasted several years, bear markets usually from a few months to about a year and a half. The app looks at the global stock ETF ACWI: a bull market when the price is above a rising 200-session average; a correction on a drop of 10-20% from the peak of the last year, a bear market on a drop of 20% or more. Now: weakness. Global stocks are below their 200-session average: a weaker trend usually weighs on growth stocks and riskier markets.

Over the years the dollar has alternately strengthened and weakened against other currencies, and one such phase usually lasted several years. It is the main currency of trade and commodities, so its exchange rate usually went together with commodity prices, emerging market results and the value of foreign assets in zloty. The app looks at the dollar index DXY (the dollar against a basket of major currencies): strengthening when the index is above its 200-session average and gained over 3% in six months; weakening in the opposite case. Now: strengthening. A strengthening dollar raises the value of USD assets in zloty and usually weighs on emerging markets and dollar-priced commodities.

A bond yield is the yearly return on lending money to a government; the 10-year US Treasury yield is the benchmark for the cost of money worldwide. The yield curve compares long bonds with short ones: long ones usually yield more, and when short ones yielded more (an inverted curve), it often came before a US recession in the past, though not always. The app looks at the 3-month change of the 10-year US Treasury yield: a move of at least 0.40 pp up means rising yields, down falling ones; it measures the curve as the difference between 10-year bonds and 3-month bills. Now: yields stable. The 10-year US Treasury yield moved less than 0.40 pp in 3 months: the cost of money is standing still.

Over the years the dollar has alternately strengthened and weakened against other currencies, and one such phase usually lasted several years. It is the main currency of trade and commodities, so its exchange rate usually went together with commodity prices, emerging market results and the value of foreign assets in zloty. The app looks at the dollar index DXY (the dollar against a basket of major currencies): strengthening when the index is above its 200-session average and gained over 3% in six months; weakening in the opposite case. Now: no trend · inverted curve. The dollar index has no clear trend: neither the six-month change nor the 200-session average points one way. The curve is inverted: 3-month bills yield more than 10-year bonds, which usually weighs on bank margins and lending.

Commodities (oil, gas, metals, crops) have their own multi-year cycles of rising and falling prices. A long wave of gains is called a supercycle: the last one came in the first decade of the 21st century, when demand from China grew fast. The app looks at a broad commodity basket, the ETF DBC: a commodity bull market when the price is above its 200-session average and over 10% higher than a year ago; a commodity bear market in the opposite case. Now: commodity bear market. A broad commodity basket is below its 200-session average and over 10% lower than a year ago: falling commodity prices usually weigh on commodity and mining companies.
